units.title: Sequences & Series

exercises.question: Number of permutations: P(5,3)
exercises.explain: There are 5 choices for the first spot, then 4, then 3, and order matters: 5 * 4 * 3 = 60.

exercises.question: Combinations C(5,2) =
exercises.explain: C(5,2) = 5!/(2! * 3!) = 120/12 = 10, because the order of the two picks does not count.

exercises.question: Combinations differ from permutations because order...
exercises.explain: Combinations ignore order, so AB and BA count as one choice. Permutations care about order.

exercises.question: Sum of first 4 terms of geometric series 2,4,8,16: S4 =
exercises.explain: Add the terms: 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30.

exercises.question: A geometric series converges when |r| is...
exercises.explain: A geometric series only converges when |r| < 1, so each term gets smaller and the sum settles down.

exercises.question: In an arithmetic sequence, a1=5 and d=3. What is a10?
exercises.explain: The nth term is a1 + (n - 1)d, so a10 = 5 + 9(3) = 32.

exercises.question: The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence is...
exercises.explain: Each term adds d to the one before, so the formula starts at a1 and adds d a total of (n - 1) times.

exercises.question: Sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic series:
exercises.explain: Average the first and last terms and multiply by the number of terms: Sn = n/2 (a1 + an).

exercises.question: An infinite geometric series converges when...
exercises.explain: An infinite geometric series converges only when |r| < 1, so the terms shrink toward zero.

exercises.question: Does the series with r = -0.99 converge or diverge?
exercises.explain: Convergence depends on |r|, and |-0.99| = 0.99 is less than 1, so the series converges.

exercises.question: Sum of an infinite geometric series with a1=8, r=1/2:

units.tip: A geometric series only converges when |r| < 1, so use the size of r, not its sign: r = -0.99 converges. Example: the sum of 8 + 4 + 2 + ... is 8/(1 - 1/2) = 16.

units.title: Transformations

exercises.question: y = f(x-3) shifts the graph of f(x)...
exercises.explain: Subtracting 3 inside the bracket moves the graph right 3, because the input has to be 3 bigger to get the same output.

exercises.question: y = -f(x) reflects f(x) over the...
exercises.explain: The minus sign flips every y-value, so the graph flips over the x-axis.

exercises.question: y = f(-x) reflects f(x) over the...
exercises.explain: Replacing x with -x flips the graph left and right, which is a reflection over the y-axis.

exercises.question: If f(x)=x^2 and g(x)=f(x)+4, what is g(2)?
y = 2f(x) is a vertical...
exercises.explain: Multiplying every y-value by 2 stretches the graph vertically by a factor of 2.

exercises.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = x + 5: f^-1(x) =
exercises.explain: Undo the +5 by subtracting: y = x + 5 gives x = y - 5, so f^-1(x) = x - 5.

exercises.question: The graph of f^-1(x) is the reflection of f(x) over...
exercises.explain: Swapping x and y reflects a graph over the line y = x.

exercises.question: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x: f^-1(x) =
exercises.explain: Swap x and y: y = 2x becomes x = 2y, so y = x/2.

exercises.question: For f^-1 to exist as a function, f must be...
exercises.explain: Only a one-to-one function has an inverse that is also a function, because each output must come from exactly one input.

exercises.question: Which function is one-to-one?
exercises.explain: y = x^3 passes the horizontal line test, since every horizontal line hits it only once. |x|, x^2 and x^4 all repeat y-values.

exercises.question: The horizontal line test checks whether a function is...
exercises.explain: If no horizontal line cuts the graph twice, the function is one-to-one.

exercises.question: Inverse of f(x) = 3x + 2: f^-1(x) =
exercises.explain: Swap x and y: x = 3y + 2, so 3y = x - 2 and y = (x - 2)/3.

exercises.question: Inverse of f(x) = x^3 + 5:
exercises.explain: Swap x and y: x = y^3 + 5, so y^3 = x - 5 and y = (x - 5)^(1/3).

exercises.question: If (2, 8) is on f(x), the point on f^-1 has x-coordinate:
exercises.explain: Inverses swap coordinates: (2, 8) on f becomes (8, 2) on f^-1, so the x-coordinate is 8.

exercises.question: To make f(x) = x^2 one-to-one, restrict the domain to
exercises.explain: On x >= 0, x^2 gives each output only once. The other domains still contain a pair like x = 1 and x = -1 that give the same output.

units.tip: In y = f(x - 3) the minus inside the bracket moves the graph right 3, which is the opposite of what it looks like. To find an inverse, swap x and y and solve: y = 3x + 2 becomes x = 3y + 2, so y = (x - 2)/3.

units.title: Polynomials

exercises.question: Divide: (x^2 - 1) / (x - 1) =
exercises.explain: Factor the top: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). Cancel the (x - 1) to get x + 1.

exercises.question: Remainder Theorem: dividing P(x) by (x-a), the remainder equals...
exercises.explain: The Remainder Theorem says the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x - a) is P(a).

exercises.question: By the Factor Theorem, (x-a) is a factor of P(x) if...
exercises.explain: If P(a) = 0 the remainder is zero, so (x - a) divides evenly and is a factor.

exercises.question: Factor: x^2 - 9 =
exercises.explain: Difference of squares: x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3).

exercises.question: Find the remainder when x^2+3x+2 is divided by (x-1)
exercises.explain: The remainder is P(1) = 1^2 + 3(1) + 2 = 6.

exercises.question: An odd-degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient: as x->infinity, y->
exercises.explain: An odd-degree polynomial with a positive leading coefficient rises to the right, so y goes to infinity as x goes to infinity.

exercises.question: How many x-intercepts (max) can a degree-4 polynomial have?
exercises.explain: A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots, so degree 4 gives at most 4 x-intercepts.

exercises.question: A root with even multiplicity touches the x-axis and...
exercises.explain: An even multiplicity means the graph touches the x-axis and turns back, so it bounces off.

exercises.question: By the remainder theorem, dividing P(x) by (x-a) gives a remainder of...
exercises.explain: Remainder Theorem: dividing P(x) by (x - a) leaves the remainder P(a).

exercises.question: (x-a) is a factor of P(x) if and only if...
exercises.explain: (x - a) is a factor exactly when P(a) = 0, because then the remainder is zero.

exercises.question: If P(x)=x^3-2x^2+x-6, what is the remainder when divided by (x-3)?
exercises.explain: P(3) = 3^3 - 2(3)^2 + 3 - 6 = 27 - 18 + 3 - 6 = 6, and that is the remainder.

exercises.question: A root of even multiplicity means the graph...
exercises.explain: An even multiplicity means the graph touches the x-axis and bounces back without crossing.

exercises.question: For an odd-degree polynomial with a negative leading coefficient, end behaviour is...
exercises.answer: up on the left, down on the right
choices: down on the left, up on the right
up on the left, down on the right
exercises.explain: Odd degree with a negative leading coefficient: the left end goes up and the right end goes down.

exercises.question: Solve 64a^3 - 16a = 0 for the positive root:
exercises.explain: Factor out 16a: 16a(4a^2 - 1) = 0, so 4a^2 = 1 and the positive root is a = 1/2.

units.tip: Remainder Theorem: the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x - a) is P(a). Example: x^2 + 3x + 2 divided by (x - 1) leaves P(1) = 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. Watch the sign: (x - 3) uses a = 3, and (x + 3) uses a = -3.

units.title: Exponents & Logarithms

exercises.question: Exponential growth model?
exercises.explain: Exponential growth and decay have the variable in the exponent: y = a * b^x.

exercises.question: If 0 < b < 1 in y = a*b^x, the function represents...
exercises.explain: When 0 < b < 1, each step multiplies by a fraction, so the value shrinks. That is decay.

exercises.question: Simplify: 2^3 * 2^2 =
exercises.explain: Same base, so add the exponents: 2^3 * 2^2 = 2^5 = 32.

exercises.question: Simplify: (x^2)^3 =
exercises.explain: Multiply the exponents: (x^2)^3 = x^(2 * 3) = x^6.

exercises.question: Evaluate: log3(27)
exercises.explain: 3 to what power gives 27? Since 3^3 = 27, log3(27) = 3.

exercises.question: Product law: log(MN) =
exercises.explain: The product law turns multiplication inside the log into addition outside: log(MN) = log M + log N.

exercises.question: Power law: log(M^k) =
exercises.explain: The power law moves the exponent out front as a multiplier: log(M^k) = k log M.

exercises.question: Solve: log2(x) = 4, x =
exercises.explain: Rewrite in exponent form: 2^4 = x, so x = 16.

exercises.question: log(ab) =
exercises.explain: The product law: the log of a product is the sum of the logs.

exercises.question: log(a^n) =
exercises.explain: The power law: the exponent n moves out front as a multiplier, so log(a^n) = n log a.

exercises.question: Change of base: log_b(x) =
exercises.explain: Change of base: log_b(x) = log(x)/log(b), using the same log base on top and bottom.

exercises.question: Solve 3^x = 11. Round to 4 decimals.
exercises.explain: Take the log of both sides: x = log(11)/log(3) = 2.3979/1.0986, which rounds to 2.1827.

exercises.question: x^(1/n) is equivalent to...
exercises.explain: The exponent 1/n means the nth root, so x^(1/n) is the nth root of x.

exercises.question: When solving a logarithmic equation you must always check for...
exercises.explain: Squaring or multiplying through can create fake answers, so check each one in the original equation.

units.tip: Log laws work on products, quotients and powers, but not on sums: log(a + b) does not simplify. Example: log2(8) + log2(4) = log2(32) = 5.

units.title: Rational Expressions & Conic Sections

exercises.question: Before simplifying a rational expression you must state the...
exercises.explain: Find and state the values that make a denominator zero before you simplify.

exercises.question: Non-permissible values are the values that make the denominator equal to...
exercises.explain: A denominator cannot be zero, so the values that make it zero are the non-permissible values.

exercises.question: Non-permissible values of (x+2)/(x^2-9):
exercises.explain: Set x^2 - 9 = 0, so (x - 3)(x + 3) = 0. Both x = 3 and x = -3 are not allowed.

exercises.question: To add two rational expressions you first find the...
exercises.explain: You need a common denominator before you add rational expressions, so you use the LCD.

exercises.question: To solve a rational equation, multiply through by the LCD and then...
choices: take the log of both sides
exercises.explain: Multiplying by the LCD can create false answers, so every answer must be checked in the original equation.

exercises.question: Simplify (x^2-4)/(x-2) for x not equal to 2:
exercises.explain: Factor the top: (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2). Cancel the (x - 2) to get x + 2 when x is not 2.

exercises.question: A plane cutting a double-napped cone perpendicular to its axis forms a...
exercises.explain: A plane cutting straight across the cone, perpendicular to the axis, makes a circle.

exercises.question: A plane parallel to one side of the cone forms a...
exercises.explain: A plane parallel to one slanted side touches only one nappe once, which gives a parabola.

exercises.question: A plane intersecting both nappes forms a...
exercises.explain: A plane cutting through both nappes gives two separate curves, which is a hyperbola.

exercises.question: Standard form of a circle centred at (h,k) with radius r:
exercises.explain: The standard form of a circle is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2, with centre (h, k) and radius r.

exercises.question: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is the standard form of a(n)...
exercises.explain: Two squared terms added and set equal to 1, with different denominators, give an ellipse.

exercises.question: Vertical asymptote of y = 1/(x - 3): x =
exercises.explain: A vertical asymptote is where the denominator is zero: x - 3 = 0, so x = 3.

exercises.question: Horizontal asymptote of y = 1/(x + 4) - 1: y =
exercises.explain: The horizontal asymptote is the constant at the end of the equation: y = -1.

exercises.question: y = (x+3)(x-5)/(x+3) has a ___ at x = -3
exercises.explain: The (x + 3) factor cancels from top and bottom, which leaves a hole at x = -3, not an asymptote.

exercises.question: y-coordinate of the hole in y = (x+3)(x-5)/(x+3):
exercises.explain: Cancel to get y = x - 5, then at x = -3: y = -3 - 5 = -8.

exercises.question: In y = (x-1)(x+2)/((x-1)(x-4)), x = 4 is a
exercises.explain: The (x - 1) cancels, but (x - 4) stays in the denominator, so x = 4 is a vertical asymptote.

exercises.question: y-coordinate of the hole in y = (x-1)(x+2)/((x-1)(x-4)):
exercises.explain: Cancel (x - 1) to get y = (x + 2)/(x - 4). At x = 1 that is 3/(-3) = -1.

units.tip: Before you simplify a rational expression, list the x-values that make the denominator zero, and keep them excluded. Example: in (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) the x = 2 value is a hole, so the simplified answer is x + 2 with x not equal to 2.

units.title: Sinusoidal Functions

exercises.question: Convert to radians: 180 deg
exercises.explain: 180 degrees is a half turn, which is pi radians.

exercises.question: Convert to radians: 90 deg
exercises.explain: 90 degrees is a quarter turn, which is pi/2 radians.

exercises.question: Exact value: sin(pi/6)
exercises.explain: On the unit circle, the point at pi/6 has y-coordinate 1/2, so sin(pi/6) = 1/2.

exercises.question: Unit circle: cos(pi/2)
exercises.explain: At pi/2 the point on the unit circle is (0, 1), so cos(pi/2) = 0.

exercises.question: Exact value: tan(pi/4)
exercises.explain: At pi/4 sin and cos are both sqrt(2)/2, so tan = sin/cos = 1.

exercises.question: Exact value: cos(pi/3)
exercises.explain: At pi/3 the point on the unit circle is (1/2, sqrt(3)/2), so cos(pi/3) = 1/2.

exercises.question: Solve: sin(x) = 1/2, 0 <= x <= 2pi
exercises.explain: Sine equals 1/2 at pi/6 in Quadrant I and at pi - pi/6 = 5pi/6 in Quadrant II.

exercises.question: Amplitude of y = 3sin(2x)
exercises.explain: The amplitude is the number in front, which is 3. The 2 inside only changes the period.

exercises.question: Period of y = sin(2x)
exercises.explain: Period = 2pi/b = 2pi/2 = pi.

exercises.question: Law of Sines?
choices: a sin(A) = b sin(B) = c sin(C)
exercises.explain: Each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same ratio. The a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos(A) choice is the cosine law.

exercises.question: Law of Cosines?
exercises.explain: The Law of Cosines: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos(C), where C is the angle opposite side c.

exercises.question: In y = a·sin(b(x-c)) + d, the amplitude is...
exercises.explain: The amplitude is |a|, the distance from the midline up to the max. It is always positive.

exercises.question: In y = a·sin(b(x-c)) + d, the period is...
exercises.explain: The period is 2pi/b, the length of one full cycle.

exercises.question: Amplitude in terms of the max and min of a sinusoid:
exercises.explain: Half the distance from min to max is the amplitude: (8 - (-8))/2 = 8.

exercises.question: The midline d equals...
exercises.explain: The midline is the average of the max and min: (max + min)/2.

exercises.question: A sinusoid with max=8, min=-8, period=π and a peak at x=0 has equation...
exercises.explain: Amplitude 8 gives a = 8, period pi gives b = 2, and a cosine starts at a peak at x = 0, so y = 8cos(2x).

exercises.question: Convert 60 degrees to radians (as a multiple of π, e.g. pi/6):
exercises.explain: Multiply by pi/180: 60 * pi/180 = pi/3.

units.tip: Degrees to radians: multiply by pi/180, so 60 degrees is 60pi/180 = pi/3. In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d the amplitude is |a|, the midline is y = d and the period is 2pi/b.

units.title: Trigonometric Identities

exercises.question: sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) =
exercises.explain: This is the Pythagorean identity. On the unit circle x^2 + y^2 = 1, so sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.

exercises.question: csc(x) is the reciprocal of...
exercises.explain: csc is 1 over sin, so csc is the reciprocal of sin.

exercises.question: 1 + tan^2(x) =
exercises.explain: Divide sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 by cos^2 to get 1 + tan^2 = sec^2.

exercises.question: sec(x) is the reciprocal of...
exercises.explain: sec is 1 over cos, so sec is the reciprocal of cos.

exercises.question: sin(A+B) = sin(A)cos(B) + ?
exercises.explain: The sine sum formula is sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

exercises.question: cos(2x) = cos^2(x) - ?
exercises.explain: cos(2x) = cos^2 x - sin^2 x, so the missing term is sin^2 x.

exercises.question: sin(2x) =
exercises.explain: The double angle formula for sine: sin(2x) = 2 sin x cos x.

exercises.question: sin 2θ =
exercises.explain: The double angle formula for sine is sin(2 theta) = 2 sin(theta) cos(theta).

exercises.question: cos 2θ written using sine only:
exercises.explain: cos(2 theta) has three forms. The one with sine only is 1 - 2sin^2(theta).

exercises.question: 1 + tan²θ =
exercises.explain: Divide sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 by cos^2 to get 1 + tan^2 = sec^2.

exercises.question: Solve 2cos²x - sinx = -1 on [0, 2π). x =
exercises.explain: Replace cos^2 x with 1 - sin^2 x: 2 - 2sin^2 x - sin x = -1, so 2sin^2 x + sin x - 3 = 0, which factors as (2 sin x + 3)(sin x - 1) = 0. Only sin x = 1 works, so x = pi/2.

exercises.question: When proving an identity, you may NOT...
exercises.answer: move terms across the equals sign
choices: rewrite in terms of sine and cosine
move terms across the equals sign
exercises.explain: You cannot assume the identity is true yet, so never move terms across the equals sign. Simplify each side on its own until they match.

exercises.question: CAST tells you which quadrants a trig ratio is...
exercises.explain: CAST says which trig ratios are positive: All in Q1, Sine in Q2, Tangent in Q3, Cosine in Q4.

exercises.question: 1 - sin^2(x) =
exercises.explain: Rearranging sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 gives cos^2 x = 1 - sin^2 x.

exercises.question: sin(x)cos(x)cot(x) simplifies to
exercises.explain: cot x = cos x/sin x, so sin x * cos x * (cos x/sin x) = cos^2 x after the sin x cancels.

exercises.question: When proving an identity you should
choices: add the same term to both sides
divide both sides by the same thing
exercises.explain: Work on each side as its own expression until both reach the same form. Cross-multiplying and adding or dividing the same thing to both sides are equation moves, not identity moves. See the problems list, because this conflicts with the answer to precalc12_u7_l3_4.

exercises.question: If sin(t) = 3/5 and t is in Q1, cos(t) =
exercises.explain: sin t = 3/5 means a 3-4-5 triangle with hypotenuse 5 and adjacent side 4. Cosine is positive in Q1, so cos t = 4/5.

exercises.question: If sin(t) = 3/4 and t is in Q2, cos(t) = -sqrt(n)/4. n =
exercises.explain: cos^2 t = 1 - (3/4)^2 = 7/16, so cos t = -sqrt(7)/4 in Q2 where cosine is negative. So n = 7.

exercises.question: cos(2x) = 2cos^2(x) - ?
exercises.explain: cos(2x) = 2cos^2 x - 1, so the missing constant is 1.

exercises.question: cos(2x) = 1 - ?sin^2(x). ? =
exercises.explain: cos(2x) = 1 - 2sin^2 x, so the missing number is 2.

exercises.question: tan(2x) = 2tan(x) / (1 - ?)
exercises.explain: The tangent double angle formula is tan(2x) = 2tan(x)/(1 - tan^2(x)).

exercises.question: If sin(t) = 3/4 and t is in Q2, sin(2t) =
exercises.explain: sin(2t) = 2 sin t cos t = 2(3/4)(-sqrt(7)/4) = -3sqrt(7)/8, since cosine is negative in Q2.

exercises.question: Best form of cos(2x) to solve cos(2x) + 1 = cos(x)
exercises.explain: Using 2cos^2 x - 1 turns the equation into 2cos^2 x = cos x, which has only cos x in it.

exercises.question: 1 + cot^2(x) =
exercises.explain: Divide sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 by sin^2 to get 1 + cot^2 = csc^2.

units.tip: Simplify one side of an identity into sines and cosines until it matches the other side. Example: sin x cos x cot x = sin x cos x (cos x / sin x) = cos^2 x.

units.title: Functions & Radicals

exercises.question: Same f and g: g(f(x)) =
exercises.explain: g(f(x)) = (x - 4)^2 + 4, because g squares its input after f has subtracted 4.

exercises.question: f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are...
exercises.explain: Test with x = 2: f(g(2)) = 4, but g(f(2)) = g(-2) = 8. The answers differ, so order matters.

exercises.question: Domain of y = sqrt(x - 3) + 1: x >=
exercises.explain: The square root needs x - 3 >= 0, so the domain is x >= 3.

exercises.question: x-coordinate of the start point of y = 2sqrt(x - 3) + 1:
exercises.explain: The start point is where the inside is zero: x - 3 = 0, so x = 3.

exercises.question: y-coordinate of the start point of y = 2sqrt(x - 3) + 1:
exercises.explain: At x = 3 the y-value is 2 sqrt(0) + 1 = 1.

exercises.question: y = -sqrt(x + 2) - 4 heads which way?
exercises.explain: The +2 inside shifts the start left to x = -2, and the minus sign flips the curve downward, so it heads down and right.

exercises.question: y = sqrt(-x) heads which way?
exercises.explain: sqrt(-x) only works for x <= 0, so the graph heads up and to the left.

exercises.question: Range of y = -sqrt(x + 2) - 4: y <=
exercises.explain: A square root never goes below its start, and the -4 puts the top at y = -4, so the range is y <= -4.

exercises.question: If (4, 9) is on f(x), which point is on sqrt(f(x))?
exercises.explain: At x = 4, sqrt(f(4)) = sqrt(9) = 3, so the point is (4, 3).

exercises.question: The graph of sqrt(f(x)) does not exist where
exercises.explain: The square root of a negative number is not a real number, so there is no graph where f(x) < 0.

exercises.question: Points stay put on sqrt(f(x)) where f(x) equals
exercises.explain: sqrt(0) = 0 and sqrt(1) = 1, so those points do not move.

units.tip: Compose inside out: f(g(2)) means find g(2) first, then put that into f. Example: with f(x) = x - 4 and g(x) = x^2 + 4, f(g(2)) = f(8) = 4 but g(f(3)) = g(-1) = 5, so order matters.

units.title: Trig Graphs & Equations

exercises.question: Period of y = sin(2x):
exercises.explain: Period = 2pi/b = 2pi/2 = pi.

exercises.question: Amplitude of y = 3sin(2(x - pi/4)) + 1:
exercises.explain: The amplitude is |3| = 3. The +1 and the shift do not change it.

exercises.question: Midline of y = 3sin(2(x - pi/4)) + 1: y =
exercises.explain: The midline is the +1 at the end, so y = 1.

exercises.question: Maximum value of y = 3sin(2(x - pi/4)) + 1:
exercises.explain: Max = midline + amplitude = 1 + 3 = 4.

exercises.question: A wave has max 5 and min -1. Its amplitude:
exercises.explain: Amplitude = (max - min)/2 = (5 - (-1))/2 = 3.

exercises.question: A wave has period pi. Its b value (2pi/period):
exercises.explain: b = 2pi/period = 2pi/pi = 2.

exercises.question: In y = sin(bx), increasing b makes the graph
exercises.explain: Multiplying x by b squeezes the graph horizontally, so each cycle is shorter.

exercises.question: tan(x) =
exercises.explain: tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) by definition.

exercises.question: y = tan(x) has vertical asymptotes where
exercises.explain: Tangent is undefined where cos(x) = 0, and those places are its vertical asymptotes.

exercises.question: Period of y = tan(x):
exercises.explain: Tangent repeats every pi, so its period is pi.

exercises.question: tan(pi/4) =
exercises.explain: At pi/4, sin and cos are both sqrt(2)/2, so tan(pi/4) = 1.

exercises.question: tan(pi/3) =
exercises.explain: At pi/3, sin = sqrt(3)/2 and cos = 1/2, so tan(pi/3) = sqrt(3).

exercises.question: tan(0) =
exercises.explain: sin(0) = 0 and cos(0) = 1, so tan(0) = 0.

exercises.question: Solve tan^2(x) - 5tan(x) + 4 = 0: smallest positive x (exact):
exercises.explain: Factor (tan x - 1)(tan x - 4) = 0, so tan x = 1 or tan x = 4. The smallest positive x with tan x = 1 is pi/4.

exercises.question: Solve 2cos^2(x) - cos(x) = 0 on [0, 2pi): smallest x:
exercises.explain: Factor cos x (2cos x - 1) = 0, so cos x = 0 or cos x = 1/2. The smallest x in [0, 2pi) is pi/3.

exercises.question: Replace cos(2x) with 2cos^2(x) - 1 in cos(2x) + 1 = cos(x) to get 2cos^2(x) =
exercises.explain: Replace cos(2x): 2cos^2 x - 1 + 1 = cos x, so 2cos^2 x = cos x.

exercises.question: Solve 2sin(2x) = -1: sin(2x) =
exercises.explain: Divide both sides by 2: sin(2x) = -1/2.

exercises.question: Solve sin(2x) = -1/2 on [0, 2pi): smallest x (exact):
exercises.explain: Let t = 2x, which runs over [0, 4pi). sin t = -1/2 first happens at t = 7pi/6, so x = 7pi/12.

exercises.question: sin(2x) = -1/2 on [0, 2pi) has how many solutions?
exercises.explain: For t in [0, 4pi), sin t = -1/2 at 7pi/6, 11pi/6, 19pi/6 and 23pi/6, which is 4 solutions for x.

units.tip: For a trig equation with an angle like 2x, solve for the whole angle over the doubled interval, then divide by 2. Example: sin(2x) = -1/2 on [0, 2pi) means 2x runs over [0, 4pi), giving 4 solutions and the smallest is x = 7pi/12.

units.title: Exponential & Log Functions

exercises.question: Horizontal asymptote of y = -2^(x+3) + 1: y =
exercises.explain: The constant +1 at the end is the horizontal asymptote, so y = 1.

exercises.question: y = -2^(x+3) + 1 is 2^x...
exercises.answer: reflected over the x-axis, left 3, up 1
choices: reflected over the y-axis, right 3, up 1
reflected over the x-axis, left 3, up 1
reflected over the x-axis, right 3, down 1
exercises.explain: The minus sign reflects over the x-axis, the (x + 3) shifts left 3, and the +1 shifts up 1.

exercises.question: Solve 8^(3x-2) = 16^(x+1): x =
exercises.explain: Write both as powers of 2: 8^(3x - 2) = 2^(9x - 6) and 16^(x + 1) = 2^(4x + 4). So 9x - 6 = 4x + 4, 5x = 10, and x = 2.

exercises.question: y = b^x with 0 < b < 1 is
exercises.explain: A base between 0 and 1 gives an exponential decay curve.

exercises.question: Vertical asymptote of y = log_2(x): x =
exercises.explain: A log is only defined for x > 0, so the vertical asymptote of log2(x) is x = 0.

exercises.question: log(a + b) equals
exercises.explain: There is no log rule for a sum, so log(a + b) stays as it is.

exercises.question: Vertical asymptote of y = -log_2(2(x + 3)): x =
exercises.explain: The log needs 2(x + 3) > 0, so the boundary is x + 3 = 0, which gives x = -3.

exercises.question: Solve 5^(x/2) = 200 (nearest hundredth): x =
exercises.explain: Take log base 5 of both sides: x/2 = log5(200) = 3.2920, so x = 6.58.

exercises.question: (1 + 1/x)^x gets close to which number as x grows?
exercises.explain: As x gets large, (1 + 1/x)^x gets close to e, about 2.718.

exercises.question: e rounded to 3 decimals:
exercises.explain: e = 2.71828..., and rounded to 3 decimals that is 2.718.

exercises.question: $1000 at 5% growing continuously for 10 years, nearest dollar: 1000e^(0.5) =
exercises.explain: Continuous growth: 1000 * e^(0.05 * 10) = 1000e^0.5 = 1648.72, which rounds to 1649.

exercises.question: Continuous growth formula
exercises.explain: Continuous growth uses base e with the rate and time in the exponent: A = A0 e^(rt).

exercises.question: Half-life is 5 days. Starting at 80 g, how many grams after 15 days?
exercises.explain: 15 days is 3 half-lives: 80 / 2 / 2 / 2 = 10 g.

exercises.question: Same sample (80 g, half-life 5 days) after 10 days, grams:
exercises.explain: 10 days is 2 half-lives: 80 / 2 / 2 = 20 g.

exercises.question: A population doubles every 3 years. Starting at 500, after 9 years:
exercises.explain: 9 years is 3 doubling periods: 500 * 2^3 = 4000.

exercises.question: A population of 200 grows 10% per year: P = 200(b)^t. b =
exercises.explain: 10% growth means each year multiplies by 1 + 0.10 = 1.1, so b = 1.1.

exercises.question: Solve 1000(1.05)^t = 2000 (nearest hundredth): t =
exercises.explain: Divide by 1000 and take logs: t = log(2)/log(1.05), which is 14.21.

exercises.question: $2000 at 3% growing continuously for 5 years, nearest dollar: 2000e^(0.15) =
exercises.explain: The rate times time is 0.03 * 5 = 0.15, so 2000e^0.15 = 2323.67, which rounds to 2324.

exercises.question: To solve a^t = c for t you
exercises.answer: take the log of both sides
choices: take the log of both sides
exercises.explain: Taking the log of both sides brings the exponent t down as a multiplier, so t = log(c)/log(a).

units.tip: To solve an exponential equation with a different base, take the log of both sides and bring the exponent down. Example: 5^(x/2) = 200 gives x/2 = log5(200), so x = 2 log5(200) = 6.58.

units.title: Final Review

exercises.question: sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) =
exercises.explain: This is the Pythagorean identity, true for every angle: sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.

exercises.question: Factor: x^2 - 16 =
exercises.explain: Difference of squares: x^2 - 16 = (x - 4)(x + 4).

units.tip: Check what the question is asking before choosing a formula. Example: 270 degrees = 270pi/180 = 3pi/2, and C(6,3) = 6!/(3! 3!) = 20, which is a count, not a sum.
